'''John Lewis Heilbron''' (March 17, 1934 – November 5, 2023) was an American [[historian of science]] best known for his work in the [[history of physics]] and the [[history of astronomy]]. He was Professor of History and Vice-Chancellor Emeritus (Vice-Chancellor 1990–1994) at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], senior research fellow at [[Worcester College, Oxford]], and visiting professor at [[Yale University]] and the [[California Institute of Technology]]. He edited the academic journal ''[[Historical Studies in the Physical and Biological Sciences]]'' for twenty-five years.

==Biography==
Born in [[San Francisco]] on March 17, 1934,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=In Memoriam, John L. Heilbron, 1934-2023 {{!}} Department of History |url=https://history.berkeley.edu/news/memoriam-john-l-heilbron-1934-2023 |access-date=2024-02-04 |website=history.berkeley.edu}}</ref> Heilbron attended [[Lowell High School (San Francisco)|Lowell High School]] in [[San Francisco, California]],<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Baggott |first=Jim |date=2023-11-21 |title=John Heilbron obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2023/nov/21/john-heilbron-obituary |access-date=2024-02-04 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> and was a member of the [[Lowell Forensic Society]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] (1955) and [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] (1958) degrees in physics and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] (1964) in history from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=":0" />  He was [[Thomas Kuhn]]'s graduate student in the 1960s when Kuhn was writing ''[[The Structure of Scientific Revolutions]].''<ref name=":1" />

Heilbron was a member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kva.se/en/Members/Kontakt-sida/?personId=647|title=The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences: John L. Heilbron|access-date=September 8, 2011|archive-date=March 28, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120328043655/http://www.kva.se/en/Members/Kontakt-sida/?personId=647|url-status=dead}}</ref> He died on November 5, 2023, at the age of 89.<ref name=":0" />

== Author ==
In addition to his university work, Heilbron authored over 20 books primarily dealing with the history of science; they included studies of phenomena such as geometry, electricity and quantum physics, as well as biographies of scientists such as [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] and [[Max Planck]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Carson |first=Cathryn |date=2024-01-23 |title=John L. Heilbron (1934–2023), historian of science |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00195-5 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=626 |issue=7997 |pages=25 |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-00195-5|pmid=38263309 |bibcode=2024Natur.626...25C |url-access=subscription }}</ref> His approach saw him investigating the influence of politics, personalities and institutions on the emergence of new scientific ideas.<ref name=":1" /> His study of the relationship between the church and science, ''The Sun in the Church: Cathedrals as Solar Observatories,'' was awarded the profession's highest prize for specific works, the [[Pfizer Award]] from the [[History of Science Society]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> He was further awarded the History of Science Society's highest award for lifetime achievement, the [[George Sarton Medal]], in 1993.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Sarton Medal |url=https://hssonline.org/page/sartonmedal |access-date=November 21, 2024 |website=History of Science Society}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* 1988: member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=John L. Heilbron |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/john-l-heilbron |access-date=April 19, 2022 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref>
* 1988: Honorary degree, [[University of Bologna]].
* 1990: member, [[American Philosophical Society]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=John+L.+Heilbron&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=April 19, 2022 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>
* 1993: awarded the [[George Sarton Medal]] by the [[History of Science Society]].<ref name=":2" />
* 2000: Honorary degree, [[University of Pavia]].
* 2006: [[Abraham Pais Prize for History of Physics]], a joint award of the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[American Institute of Physics]].
* 2006: [[Wilkins Lecture|Wilkins Prize Lecture]] of the [[Royal Society|Royal Society of London]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Benjamin Franklin in Europe: electrician, academician, politician {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/science-events-and-lectures/2006/benjamin-franklin/ |access-date=2024-02-04 |website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>

==Main books==
* 2024: ''Quantum Drama: From the [[Niels Bohr|Bohr]]-[[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] Debate to the Riddle of [[Quantum entanglement|Entanglement]]'' with [[Jim Baggott]] [[Oxford University Press]]. {{ISBN|9780192846105}}
* 2022: ''The Incomparable Monsignor: [[Francesco Bianchini]]'s World of Science, History, and Court Intrigue.'' [[Oxford University Press]]. {{ISBN|9780192856654}}
* 2021: ''The Ghost of [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] in a Forgotten Painting from the English Civil War.'' Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|9780198861300}}
* 2020: '' Niels Bohr: A Very Short Introduction'', Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|9780198819264}}
* 2018: ''The History of Physics: A Very Short Introduction'', Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|978-0199684120}}
* 2013: ''Love, Literature, and the [[Quantum]] [[Atom]]'', with Finn Aaserud, Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|9780199680283}}
* 2010: ''Galileo'', Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-958352-8}}.<ref>{{cite news|author=Gingerich, Owen|author-link=Owen Gingerich|date=December 24, 2010|newspaper=NY Times|title=Starry Messenger (joint review of ''Galileo'' by J. L. Heilbron and ''Galileo: Watcher of the Skies'' by David Wootton)|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/26/books/review/Gingerich-t.html}} (See [[David Wootton (historian)|David Wootton]].)</ref> (See [[Galileo Galilei]].)
* 2003: ''[[The Oxford Companion to the History of Modern Science]]'' (ed.), Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-511229-6}}.
* 2003: ''[[Ernest Rutherford]] and the Explosion of Atoms'', [[Oxford Portraits in Science]], Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-512378-6}}.
* 1999: ''The Sun in the Church: Cathedrals as [[Solar observatory|Solar Observatories]].'' [[Harvard University Press]]. {{ISBN|0-674-85433-0}}. 2001 paperback: {{ISBN|0-674-00536-8}}.
* 1999: ''Electricity in the 17th and 18th Centuries: A Study of Early Modern Physics.'' [[Dover Publications]]. {{ISBN|0-486-40688-1}}.
* 1997: ''Geometry Civilized: History, Culture, Technique.'' Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-850078-5}}. 2000 paperback: {{ISBN|0-19-850690-2}}.
* 1989: ''[[Ernest Lawrence|Lawrence]] and His Laboratory: A History of the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory]]'', with Robert W. Seidel. [[University of California Press]]. {{ISBN|0-520-06426-7}}.
* 1986: ''The Dilemmas of an Upright Man: [[Max Planck]] and the Fortunes of German Science'', University of California Press. {{ISBN|0-520-05710-4}}
* 1979: ''Electricity in the 17th and 18th Centuries: A Study of Early Modern Physics'', University of California Press. {{ISBN|0-520-03478-3}}.
* 1974: ''[[Henry Moseley|H. G. J. Moseley]]: The Life and Letters of an English Physicist, 1887-1915'', University of California Press. {{ISBN|0-520-02375-7}}.
